title: Game Developer: the rise of games you mostly don't play (Pecorella GDC talk write-up)
label: practitioner
claim: Quotes Pecorella: constant positive growth means no need to play constantly; a quick check-in shifts the growth curve and makes 'a celebratory moment every time that you return'; the longer away, the greater the incentive to return; idle games are a 'natural energy system' without an energy currency. Press write-up, not the slides.

title: Pecorella, Quest for Progress (GDC Europe 2016 slides), slide text via fetch
label: developer
claim: Idle games: progress without interaction, players leave the game alone regularly, no end. Quantic Foundry: motivated by Completion and Power. Egg Inc capped offline earning at 2 hours, which the speaker calls a mistake he churned over. Costs grow exponentially, production linearly; prestige rule of thumb reset at roughly +50% to +200% prestige currency; optimal purchase should be an interesting choice.

title: Pecorella, The Math of Idle Games Part I (MIGS 2016 write-up), via fetch summary
label: developer
claim: Costs grow exponentially while production grows linearly or polynomially; multipliers '(temporarily) get production closer to, or ahead of, costs'. The pacing signal is the wait for the next purchase growing 'prohibitively long'. Model progression in a spreadsheet before playtesting ('estimate progression patterns without manually playing the game'). Milestone multipliers cause purchase spikes; tune them so different generators take priority, for 'more variety and less predictability'. Check a cheap gain is felt, not just optimal. 2026-11-08 verification read of Part I: per-generator income is plotted and 'the newest generator is nearly always dominant once it can be purchased'; a model player buying the best income-to-cost item means 'players will roughly be in this ballpark', 'players usually buy in bulk', and 'higher-end, slower generators get over-favored'.

title: Pecorella, The Math of Idle Games Part III (prestige), via fetch summary
label: developer
claim: Prestige exists to create the 'ladder climbing' effect and to 'rein growth back into a more manageable number'. Prestige currency takes a root or log of earnings (AdVenture Capitalist square root, Cookie Clicker cube root: double the currency needs ~8x the earnings; Egg Inc ~1/7 power). Some games later 'added systems that do substantially rein in numbers'. Models are rough guides: 'you should not use this model as an accurate simulation'. 2026-11-08 verification read: 'similar variation in your prestige resets' (bumpy cycles); 'a player who just hit a big milestone is likely to keep going for a while since that's a fast section of the game', so prestige models mispredict right after a milestone; Egg's sub-prestige loop is called 'staircase tiers'.

title: Pecorella, Idle Chatter (GDC 2016 slides), all 127 slides as text via web.archive.org/web/2017/<this url> (slideshare blocks bots); chart images not seen; slides 100-123 are plot, spin-offs and genre blends
label: developer
claim: Constant growth 'creates a celebratory moment every time you return' and makes 'forced appointment mechanics ... unnecessary' (slide 21). 'Smooth curves are boring, lack surprise and delight' (31). 'Give players targets to aim for beyond just making bigger numbers' (81); build goals give 'clear aspirational goals' (68). Auto-clickers: 'not cheating, this is an error in design'; 'Don't have the optimal strategy require clicking constantly' (87-90). Offline: 'Calculate offline the same as online'; well-designed games without offline limits 'have great retention anyway' (92-93).

title: Pecorella, The Math of Idle Games Part II (generator chains)
label: developer
claim: Generators that make generators follow x^n/n! and always lag exponential cost; free produced units make buying lower tiers pointless, so cost on purchased count and give per-purchase tier boosts.

title: Spiel et al., 'It Started as a Joke': On the Design of Idle Games, CHI PLAY 2019
label: research
claim: Six idle designers interviewed: idle games are explorative systems of local and global optimisation with 'little consequences of failure'; new layered systems should change decisions. Verification read of the PDF: a designer (Frank Lantz) says how a new system 'fits into the existing economy ... should change my decision making'; and 'User interfaces that signal the effects of changes without actually making them, such as those provided by the tool tips and chat channels for Kittens, are another way to facilitate player safety.'

title: Demaine et al., Cookie Clicker, Graphs and Combinatorics 2020
label: research
claim: Abstract: 'ideas from NP-hardness, approximation algorithms, and dynamic programming'. Paper body (2026-11-08 verification read): the k-item fixed-cost case has a weakly polynomial dynamic program, the increasing-cost case a strongly polynomial one; a greedy algorithm is an additional approximation whose ratio approaches 1; some variants are weakly NP-hard; only the discrete-timestep version is strongly NP-hard. Used to say the pure buy-order problem has a simple greedy near-optimum, inference.

Single reviewer.
